They said that if I had been a criminal, I might have made my fortune by looking so like an honest man; but as I had the misfortune to be an honest man, there was not even the remotest chance of my assisting them by ever looking like a criminal. But at last I was brought before some old josser who was high up in the force, and who seemed to have no end of a head on his shoulders. And there the others all talked hopelessly. One asked whether a bushy beard would hide my nice smile; another said that if they blacked my face I might look like a negro anarchist; but this old chap chipped in with a most extraordinary remark. ‘A pair of smoked spectacles will do it,’ he said positively. ‘Look at him now; he looks like an angelic office boy. Put him on a pair of smoked spectacles, and children will scream at the sight of him.’ And so it was, by George! When once my eyes were covered, all the rest, smile and big shoulders and short hair, made me look a perfect little devil. As I say, it was simple enough when it was done, like miracles; but that wasn’t the really miraculous part of it. There was one really staggering thing about the business, and my head still turns at it.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: What was that?

speaker: the man
quoted_text: I’ll tell you, This big pot in the police who sized me up so that he knew how the goggles would go with my hair and socks—by God, he never saw me at all!

speaker: the man
quoted_text: How was that?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I thought you talked to him.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: So I did, but we talked in a pitch-dark room like a coalcellar. There, you would never have guessed that.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I could not have conceived it,

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: It is indeed a new idea,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I had already arranged, to go to France for my lunch; but I am delighted to have someone to lunch with me. You see, I had to send that beast, the Marquis, over with his bomb, because the President had his eye on me, though God knows how. I’ll tell you the story some day. It was perfectly choking. Whenever I tried to slip out of it I saw the President somewhere, smiling out of the bow-window of a club, or taking off his hat to me from the top of an omnibus. I tell you, you can say what you like, that fellow sold himself to the devil; he can be in six places at once.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: So you sent the Marquis off, I understand, Was it long ago? Shall we be in time to catch him?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Yes, I’ve timed it all. He’ll still be at Calais when we arrive.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: But when we do catch him at Calais, what are we going to do?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Theoretically, I suppose, we ought to call the police.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Not I, Theoretically I ought to drown myself first. I promised a poor fellow, who was a real modern pessimist, on my word of honour not to tell the police. I’m no hand at casuistry, but I can’t break my word to a modern pessimist. It’s like breaking one’s word to a child.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I’m in the same boat, I tried to tell the police and I couldn’t, because of some silly oath I took. You see, when I was an actor I was a sort of all-round beast. Perjury or treason is the only crime I haven’t committed. If I did that I shouldn’t know the difference between right and wrong.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I’ve been through all that, and I’ve made up my mind. I gave my promise to the Secretary—you know him, man who smiles upside down. My friends, that man is the most utterly unhappy man that was ever human. It may be his digestion, or his conscience, or his nerves, or his philosophy of the universe, but he’s damned, he’s in hell! Well, I can’t turn on a man like that, and hunt him down. It’s like whipping a leper. I may be mad, but that’s how I feel; and there’s jolly well the end of it.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I don’t think you’re mad, I knew you would decide like that when first you—

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Eh?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: When first you took off your spectacles.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, it seems that we have all the same kind of morality or immorality, so we had better face the fact that comes of it.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Yes, you’re quite right; and we must hurry up, for I can see the Grey Nose standing out from France.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: The fact that comes of it, is this, that we three are alone on this planet. Gogol has gone, God knows where; perhaps the President has smashed him like a fly. On the Council we are three men against three, like the Romans who held the bridge. But we are worse off than that, first because they can appeal to their organization and we cannot appeal to ours, and second because—

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Because one of those other three men, is not a man. My idea is this. We must do something to keep the Marquis in Calais till tomorrow midday. I have turned over twenty schemes in my head. We cannot denounce him as a dynamiter; that is agreed. We cannot get him detained on some trivial charge, for we should have to appear; he knows us, and he would smell a rat. We cannot pretend to keep him on anarchist business; he might swallow much in that way, but not the notion of stopping in Calais while the Czar went safely through Paris. We might try to kidnap him, and lock him up ourselves; but he is a well-known man here. He has a whole bodyguard of friends; he is very strong and brave, and the event is doubtful. The only thing I can see to do is actually to take advantage of the very things that are in the Marquis’s favour. I am going to profit by the fact that he is a highly respected nobleman. I am going to profit by the fact that he has many friends and moves in the best society.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: What the devil are you talking about?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: The Symes are first mentioned in the fourteenth century, but there is a tradition that one of them rode behind Bruce at Bannockburn. Since 1350 the tree is quite clear.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He’s gone off his head,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Our bearings, are ‘argent a chevron gules charged with three cross crosslets of the field.’ The motto varies.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: We are just inshore, Are you seasick or joking in the wrong place?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: My remarks are almost painfully practical, The house of St. Eustache also is very ancient. The Marquis cannot deny that he is a gentleman. He cannot deny that I am a gentleman. And in order to put the matter of my social position quite beyond a doubt, I propose at the earliest opportunity to knock his hat off. But here we are in the harbour. I shall approach. Before taking off his hat, I shall take off my own. I shall say, ‘The Marquis de Saint Eustache, I believe.’ He will say, ‘The celebrated Mr. Syme, I presume.’ He will say in the most exquisite French, ‘How are you?’ I shall reply in the most exquisite Cockney, ‘Oh, just the Syme—’

speaker: the man
quoted_text: Oh, shut it, Pull yourself together, and chuck away that bit of paper. What are you really going to do?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: But it was a lovely catechism, Do let me read it you. It has only forty-three questions and answers, and some of the Marquis’s answers are wonderfully witty. I like to be just to my enemy.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: But what’s the good of it all?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: It leads up to my challenge, don’t you see, When the Marquis has given the thirty-ninth reply, which runs—

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Has it by any chance occurred to you, that the Marquis may not say all the forty-three things you have put down for him? In that case, I understand, your own epigrams may appear somewhat more forced.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Why, how true that is, and I never thought of it. Sir, you have an intellect beyond the common. You will make a name.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Oh, you’re as drunk as an owl!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: It only remains, to adopt some other method of breaking the ice (if I may so express it) between myself and the man I wish to kill. And since the course of a dialogue cannot be predicted by one of its parties alone (as you have pointed out with such recondite acumen), the only thing to be done, I suppose, is for the one party, as far as possible, to do all the dialogue by himself. And so I will, by George!

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Are you going to address the meeting?

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I am, that meeting. That meeting displeases me. I am going to pull that meeting’s great ugly, mahogany-coloured nose.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: You are Mr. Syme, I think,

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: And you are the Marquis de Saint Eustache, Permit me to pull your nose.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: This man has insulted me!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Insulted you? when?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Oh, just now, He insulted my mother.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Insulted your mother!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, anyhow, my aunt.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: But how can the Marquis have insulted your aunt just now?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He has been sitting here all the time.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Ah, it was what he said!

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: I said nothing at all, except something about the band. I only said that I liked Wagner played well.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: It was an allusion to my family, My aunt played Wagner badly. It was a painful subject. We are always being insulted about it.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: This seems most extraordinary,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Oh, I assure you, the whole of your conversation was simply packed with sinister allusions to my aunt’s weaknesses.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: This is nonsense!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I for one have said nothing for half an hour except that I liked the singing of that girl with black hair.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, there you are again!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: My aunt’s was red.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: It seems to me, that you are simply seeking a pretext to insult the Marquis.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: By George! what a clever chap you are!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Seeking a quarrel with me!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Seeking a fight with me! By God! there was never a man who had to seek long. These gentlemen will perhaps act for me. There are still four hours of daylight. Let us fight this evening.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Marquis, your action is worthy of your fame and blood. Permit me to consult for a moment with the gentlemen in whose hands I shall place myself.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I have done it, I have fixed a fight on the beast. But look here, and listen carefully. There is no time for talk. You are my seconds, and everything must come from you. Now you must insist, and insist absolutely, on the duel coming off after seven tomorrow, so as to give me the chance of preventing him from catching the 7.45 for Paris. If he misses that he misses his crime. He can’t refuse to meet you on such a small point of time and place. But this is what he will do. He will choose a field somewhere near a wayside station, where he can pick up the train. He is a very good swordsman, and he will trust to killing me in time to catch it. But I can fence well too, and I think I can keep him in play, at any rate, until the train is lost. Then perhaps he may kill me to console his feelings. You understand? Very well then, let me introduce you to some charming friends of mine,

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: To a man of the well-known skill and valour of Monsieur de St. Eustache, it must be a matter of indifference which method is adopted, and our principal has strong reasons for demanding the longer encounter, reasons the delicacy of which prevent me from being explicit, but for the just and honourable nature of which I can— _Peste!_ let us stop talking and begin,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Engage!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: After all, I am more than a devil; I am a man. I can do the one thing which Satan himself cannot do—I can die,

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Stop!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I want to say something.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What is the matter?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Has there been foul play?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: There has been foul play somewhere, Our principal has wounded the Marquis four times at least, and he is none the worse.

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Please let me speak,

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: It is rather important. Mr. Syme, we are fighting today, if I remember right, because you expressed a wish (which I thought irrational) to pull my nose. Would you oblige me by pulling my nose now as quickly as possible? I have to catch a train.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I protest that this is most irregular,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It is certainly somewhat opposed to precedent, There is, I think, one case on record (Captain Bellegarde and the Baron Zumpt) in which the weapons were changed in the middle of the encounter at the request of one of the combatants. But one can hardly call one’s nose a weapon.

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Will you or will you not pull my nose?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Come, come, Mr. Syme! You wanted to do it, do it! You can have no conception of how important it is to me. Don’t be so selfish! Pull my nose at once, when I ask you!

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: If anyone has any use for my left eyebrow, he can have it. Colonel Ducroix, do accept my left eyebrow! It’s the kind of thing that might come in useful any day,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: If I had known, that I was acting for a poltroon who pads himself to fight—

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Oh, I know, I know!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You are making a mistake; but it can’t be explained just now. I tell you the train has come into the station!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Yes, and the train shall go out of the station. It shall go out without you. We know well enough for what devil’s work—

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Will you drive me mad?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: The train—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: You shall not go by the train,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: You great fat, blasted, blear-eyed, blundering, thundering, brainless, Godforsaken, doddering, damned fool!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You great silly, pink-faced, towheaded turnip! You— You shall not go by this train, And why the infernal blazes, should I want to go by the train?

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: We know all, You are going to Paris to throw a bomb!

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Going to Jericho to throw a Jabberwock!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Have you all got softening of the brain, that you don’t realise what I am? Did you really think I wanted to catch that train? Twenty Paris trains might go by for me. Damn Paris trains!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Then what did you care about?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What did I care about? I didn’t care about catching the train; I cared about whether the train caught me, and now, by God! it has caught me.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I regret to inform you, that your remarks convey no impression to my mind. Perhaps if you were to remove the remains of your original forehead and some portion of what was once your chin, your meaning would become clearer. Mental lucidity fulfils itself in many ways. What do you mean by saying that the train has caught you? It may be my literary fancy, but somehow I feel that it ought to mean something.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: It means everything, and the end of everything. Sunday has us now in the hollow of his hand.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Us!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What do you mean by ‘us’?

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: The police, of course!

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: I am Inspector Ratcliffe, My name is pretty well known to the police, and I can see well enough that you belong to them. But if there is any doubt about my position, I have a card,

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Oh, don’t show it us, we’ve got enough of them to equip a paper-chase.

speaker: the Marquis
quoted_text: Gentlemen, we all owe you a serious apology; but I assure you that you have not been made the victims of such a low joke as you imagine, or indeed of anything undignified in a man of honour. You have not wasted your time; you have helped to save the world. We are not buffoons, but very desperate men at war with a vast conspiracy. A secret society of anarchists is hunting us like hares; not such unfortunate madmen as may here or there throw a bomb through starvation or German philosophy, but a rich and powerful and fanatical church, a church of eastern pessimism, which holds it holy to destroy mankind like vermin. How hard they hunt us you can gather from the fact that we are driven to such disguises as those for which I apologise, and to such pranks as this one by which you suffer.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Of course, I accept the apology; but you will in your turn forgive me if I decline to follow you further into your difficulties, and permit myself to say good morning! The sight of an acquaintance and distinguished fellow-townsman coming to pieces in the open air is unusual, and, upon the whole, sufficient for one day. Colonel Ducroix, I would in no way influence your actions, but if you feel with me that our present society is a little abnormal, I am now going to walk back to the town.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, by George! I won’t. If these gentlemen are really in a mess with a lot of low wreckers like that, I’ll see them through it. I have fought for France, and it is hard if I can’t fight for civilization.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Don’t make too much noise, Sunday may hear you.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Sunday!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Yes, he may be with them.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: With whom?

speaker: the other
quoted_text: With the people out of that train, What you say seems utterly wild,

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Why, as a matter of fact—But, my God, by God! if this is true the whole bally lot of us on the Anarchist Council were against anarchy! Every born man was a detective except the President and his personal secretary. What can it mean?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Mean!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It means that we are struck dead! Don’t you know Sunday? Don’t you know that his jokes are always so big and simple that one has never thought of them? Can you think of anything more like Sunday than this, that he should put all his powerful enemies on the Supreme Council, and then take care that it was not supreme? I tell you he has bought every trust, he has captured every cable, he has control of every railway line—especially of _that_ railway line!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: The whole movement was controlled by him; half the world was ready to rise for him. But there were just five people, perhaps, who would have resisted him... and the old devil put them on the Supreme Council, to waste their time in watching each other. Idiots that we are, he planned the whole of our idiocies! Sunday knew that the Professor would chase Syme through London, and that Syme would fight me in France. And he was combining great masses of capital, and seizing great lines of telegraphy, while we five idiots were running after each other like a lot of confounded babies playing blind man’s buff.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well?

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Well, he has found us playing blind man’s buff today in a field of great rustic beauty and extreme solitude. He has probably captured the world; it only remains to him to capture this field and all the fools in it. And since you really want to know what was my objection to the arrival of that train, I will tell you. My objection was that Sunday or his Secretary has just this moment got out of it.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It was a habit of the late Marquis de St. Eustache, always to carry a pair of opera glasses. Either the President or the Secretary is coming after us with that mob. They have caught us in a nice quiet place where we are under no temptations to break our oaths by calling the police. Dr. Bull, I have a suspicion that you will see better through these than through your own highly decorative spectacles.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: It cannot be as bad as you say, There are a good number of them certainly, but they may easily be ordinary tourists.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Do ordinary tourists, wear black masks half-way down the face?

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: The President is not with them, anyhow,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: But surely they are right away on the horizon, Could you possibly know your President among all those people?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Could I know a white elephant among all those people!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: As you very truly say, they are on the horizon; but if he were walking with them... by God! I believe this ground would shake.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Of course the President isn’t with them. I wish to Gemini he were. Much more likely the President is riding in triumph through Paris, or sitting on the ruins of St. Paul’s Cathedral.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: This is absurd!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Something may have happened in our absence; but he cannot have carried the world with a rush like that. It is quite true, it is certainly true that there seems to be a crowd coming this way; but they are not all the army that you make out.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Oh, they, no, they are not a very valuable force. But let me tell you frankly that they are precisely calculated to our value—we are not much, my boy, in Sunday’s universe. He has got hold of all the cables and telegraphs himself. But to kill the Supreme Council he regards as a trivial matter, like a post card; it may be left to his private secretary, There is a great deal to be said for death; but if anyone has any preference for the other alternative, I strongly advise him to walk after me.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: May I ask, where on earth we are all going to?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: We must get down through the town of Lancy to the sea, I think that part of the country is least likely to be with them.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: What can you mean by all this?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: They can’t be running the real world in that way. Surely not many working men are anarchists, and surely if they were, mere mobs could not beat modern armies and police.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Mere mobs!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: So you talk about mobs and the working classes as if they were the question. You’ve got that eternal idiotic idea that if anarchy came it would come from the poor. Why should it? The poor have been rebels, but they have never been anarchists; they have more interest than anyone else in there being some decent government. The poor man really has a stake in the country. The rich man hasn’t; he can go away to New Guinea in a yacht. The poor have sometimes objected to being governed badly; the rich have always objected to being governed at all. Aristocrats were always anarchists, as you can see from the barons’ wars.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: As a lecture on English history for the little ones, this is all very nice; but I have not yet grasped its application.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Its application is, that most of old Sunday’s right-hand men are South African and American millionaires. That is why he has got hold of all the communications; and that is why the last four champions of the anti-anarchist police force are running through a wood like rabbits.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Millionaires I can understand, they are nearly all mad. But getting hold of a few wicked old gentlemen with hobbies is one thing; getting hold of great Christian nations is another. I would bet the nose off my face (forgive the allusion) that Sunday would stand perfectly helpless before the task of converting any ordinary healthy person anywhere.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Well, it rather depends what sort of person you mean.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, for instance, he could never convert that person,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Mr. Syme is saying, that this man, at least, will never be an anarchist.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Mr. Syme is right enough there, if only for the reason that he has plenty of property to defend. But I forgot that in your country you are not used to peasants being wealthy.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He looks poor,

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Quite so, that is why he is rich.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I have an idea, how much would he take to give us a lift in his cart? Those dogs are all on foot, and we could soon leave them behind.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Oh, give him anything!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I have piles of money on me.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: That will never do, he will never have any respect for you unless you drive a bargain.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Oh, if he haggles!

speaker: the other
quoted_text: He haggles because he is a free man, You do not understand; he would not see the meaning of generosity. He is not being tipped.

speaker: the policeman
quoted_text: Yes, that’s discipline. That’s Sunday. He is perhaps five hundred miles off, but the fear of him is on all of them, like the finger of God. Yes, they are walking regularly; and you bet your boots that they are talking regularly, yes, and thinking regularly. But the one important thing for us is that they are disappearing regularly.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Le Soleil d’Or.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: May I ask you, Colonel, why we have come here?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: For two reasons, sir, and I will give first, not the most important, but the most utilitarian. We came here because this is the only place within twenty miles in which we can get horses.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Horses!

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Yes, if you people are really to distance your enemies it is horses or nothing for you, unless of course you have bicycles and motor-cars in your pocket.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: And where do you advise us to make for?

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Beyond question, you had better make all haste to the police station beyond the town. My friend, whom I seconded under somewhat deceptive circumstances, seems to me to exaggerate very much the possibilities of a general rising; but even he would hardly maintain, I suppose, that you were not safe with the gendarmes. And your other reason for coming here?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: My other reason for coming here, is that it is just as well to see a good man or two when one is possibly near to death. You are right, Has anyone seen about the horses?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Yes, you may be quite certain that I gave orders the moment I came in. Those enemies of yours gave no impression of hurry, but they were really moving wonderfully fast, like a well-trained army. I had no idea that the anarchists had so much discipline. You have not a moment to waste.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Four out of the five rich men in this town, are common swindlers. I suppose the proportion is pretty equal all over the world. The fifth is a friend of mine, and a very fine fellow; and what is even more important from our point of view, he owns a motor-car.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I am afraid,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I am afraid we have hardly time for afternoon calls.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Doctor Renard’s house is only three minutes off,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Our danger, is not two minutes off.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Yes, if we ride on fast we must leave them behind, for they are on foot.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: He has a motor-car,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: But we may not get it, Yes, he is quite on your side.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: But he might be out.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Hold your tongue, What is that noise?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: They have done us, Prepare to receive cavalry!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Where can they have got the horses? I was speaking with strict accuracy when I said that the ‘Soleil d’Or’ was the only place where one can get horses within twenty miles.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: No!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I don’t believe he’d do it. Not with all that white hair.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: He may have been forced, They must be at least a hundred strong, for which reason we are all going to see my friend Renard, who has a motor-car.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Anarchy, it is childishness!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: _Et ça_, and that is childishness, isn’t it?

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: I am sorry to cut short a cultured discussion, but can you lend me your motor-car now, in two minutes?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I have a suspicion that you are all mad, but God forbid that madness should in any way interrupt friendship. Let us go round to the garage.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It is now or never, I hear horses.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, a horse.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I am afraid it’s no go.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I can’t understand why it has grown so dark,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Going to be a storm, I think, I say, it’s a pity we haven’t got a light on this car, if only to see by.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: We have,

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Where on earth did you get that?

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: I got it where I got the car, from my best friend. While our friend here was fighting with the steering wheel, I ran up the front steps of the house and spoke to Renard, who was standing in his own porch, you will remember. ‘I suppose,’ I said, ‘there’s no time to get a lamp.’ He looked up, blinking amiably at the beautiful arched ceiling of his own front hall. From this was suspended, by chains of exquisite ironwork, this lantern, one of the hundred treasures of his treasure house. By sheer force he tore the lamp out of his own ceiling, shattering the painted panels, and bringing down two blue vases with his violence. Then he handed me the iron lantern, and I put it in the car. Was I not right when I said that Dr. Renard was worth knowing?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: You were,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: These lights make one feel more cheerful.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: There is only one set of lights that make me more cheerful, and they are those lights of the police station which I can see beyond the town. Please God we may be there in ten minutes.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Oh, this is all raving nonsense!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: If you really think that ordinary people in ordinary houses are anarchists, you must be madder than an anarchist yourself. If we turned and fought these fellows, the whole town would fight for us.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: No, the whole town would fight for them. We shall see.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: What is that noise?

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Oh, the horses behind us, I suppose, I thought we had got clear of them.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: The horses behind us! No, it is not horses, and it is not behind us.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I tell you they were his, and they were full of men in masks!

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: Absurd!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Dr. Renard would never give them his cars.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He may have been forced, The whole town is on their side.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: You still believe that,

speaker: the other
quoted_text: You will all believe it soon,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, I can’t believe it. The thing is nonsense. The plain people of a peaceable French town—

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: My God! someone has shot at us.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It need not interrupt conversation, Pray resume your remarks, Colonel. You were talking, I think, about the plain people of a peaceable French town.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: It is extraordinary, most extraordinary.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: A fastidious person, might even call it unpleasant. However, I suppose those lights out in the field beyond this street are the Gendarmerie. We shall soon get there.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, we shall never get there.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What do you mean?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I mean that we shall never get there, They have two rows of armed men across the road already; I can see them from here. The town is in arms, as I said it was. I can only wallow in the exquisite comfort of my own exactitude.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It is quite true. There is a crowd or an army or some such thing across the end of that street.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Well, if there is, it must be something else—a sham fight or the mayor’s birthday or something. I cannot and will not believe that plain, jolly people in a place like this walk about with dynamite in their pockets. Get on a bit, Syme, and let us look at them.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Why, you silly mugs! what did I tell you. That crowd’s as law-abiding as a cow, and if it weren’t, it’s on our side.

speaker: the professor
quoted_text: How do you know?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You blind bat, don’t you see who is leading them?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Why, it’s Renard!

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: What a fool I’ve been!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Of course, the dear old boy has turned out to help us.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Dr. Renard! Dr. Renard!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Well, what do you think now?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I think, that I am lying in bed at No. 217 Peabody Buildings, and that I shall soon wake up with a jump; or, if that’s not it, I think that I am sitting in a small cushioned cell in Hanwell, and that the doctor can’t make much of my case. But if you want to know what I don’t think, I’ll tell you. I don’t think what you think. I don’t think, and I never shall think, that the mass of ordinary men are a pack of dirty modern thinkers. No, sir, I’m a democrat, and I still don’t believe that Sunday could convert one average navvy or counter-jumper. No, I may be mad, but humanity isn’t.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: You are a very fine fellow, You can believe in a sanity which is not merely your sanity. And you’re right enough about humanity, about peasants and people like that jolly old innkeeper. But you’re not right about Renard. I suspected him from the first. He’s rationalistic, and, what’s worse, he’s rich. When duty and religion are really destroyed, it will be by the rich.

speaker: the man
quoted_text: They are really destroyed now, The devils are coming on!

speaker: the man
quoted_text: Gentlemen, the thing is incredible. It must be a practical joke. If you knew Renard as I do—it’s like calling Queen Victoria a dynamiter. If you had got the man’s character into your head—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Dr. Bull, has at least got it into his hat.

speaker: the Colonel
quoted_text: I tell you it can’t be!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Renard shall explain it. He shall explain it to me, Don’t be in such a hurry, He will very soon explain it to all of us.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: It is no good, He will never get anything out of that old heathen. I vote we drive bang through the thick of them, bang as the bullets went through Bull’s hat. We may all be killed, but we must kill a tidy number of them.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I won’t ’ave it, The poor chaps may be making a mistake. Give the Colonel a chance.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Shall we go back, then?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, the street behind us is held too. In fact, I seem to see there another friend of yours, Syme.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: What the devil is up?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: The morning star has fallen!

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: The world is insane!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, it is I.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: What are we going to do?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: At this moment, I think we are going to smash into a lamppost.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Well, we smashed something, That’s some comfort.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: You’re becoming an anarchist,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Everyone is,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: We have one more chance, Whatever all this pandemonium means, I suppose the police station will help us. We can’t get there, for they hold the way. But there’s a pier or breakwater runs out into the sea just here, which we could defend longer than anything else, like Horatius and his bridge. We must defend it till the Gendarmerie turn out. Keep after me.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: The peasant!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: They have not risen since the Middle Ages.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Even if the police do come now, they can do nothing with this mob.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Nonsense! there must be some people left in the town who are human.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, the human being will soon be extinct. We are the last of mankind.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: It may be, What is all that at the end of the ‘Dunciad’? ‘Nor public flame; nor private, dares to shine; Nor human light is left, nor glimpse divine! Lo! thy dread Empire, Chaos, is restored; Light dies before thine uncreating word: Thy hand, great Anarch, lets the curtain fall; And universal darkness buries all.’

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Stop! the gendarmes are out.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: They are charging the mob!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: No, they are formed along the parade.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: They have unslung their carbines,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Yes, and they are going to fire on us.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: The gendarmes have joined them!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I am in the padded cell,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What does it matter who is mad or who is sane? We shall all be dead soon.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You are quite hopeless, then?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No; oddly enough I am not quite hopeless. There is one insane little hope that I cannot get out of my mind. The power of this whole planet is against us, yet I cannot help wondering whether this one silly little hope is hopeless yet.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: In what or whom is your hope?

speaker: the other
quoted_text: In a man I never saw,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I know what you mean, the man in the dark room. But Sunday must have killed him by now.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Perhaps, but if so, he was the only man whom Sunday found it hard to kill.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I heard what you said, I also am holding hard on to the thing I never saw.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Where is the Colonel? I thought he was with us!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: The Colonel! Yes, where on earth is the Colonel?

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: He went to speak to Renard,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: We cannot leave him among all those beasts, Let us die like gentlemen if—

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Do not pity the Colonel, He is extremely comfortable. He is—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: No! no! no! not the Colonel too! I will never believe it!

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Will you believe your eyes?

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Yes, he is gone too, Everything’s gone. I’m gone! I can’t trust my own bodily machinery. I feel as if my own hand might fly up and strike me.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: When my hand flies up, it will strike somebody else,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Judas before Herod!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Do you see this lantern?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Do you see the cross carved on it, and the flame inside? You did not make it. You did not light it. Better men than you, men who could believe and obey, twisted the entrails of iron and preserved the legend of fire. There is not a street you walk on, there is not a thread you wear, that was not made as this lantern was, by denying your philosophy of dirt and rats. You can make nothing. You can only destroy. You will destroy mankind; you will destroy the world. Let that suffice you. Yet this one old Christian lantern you shall not destroy. It shall go where your empire of apes will never have the wit to find it.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Swords!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Let us charge these dogs, for our time has come to die.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: There is some mistake, Mr. Syme, I hardly think you understand your position. I arrest you in the name of the law.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Of the law?

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Certainly!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I am a detective from Scotland Yard,

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: And what do you suppose we are?

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: You, are, as I know for a fact, members of the Supreme Anarchist Council. Disguised as one of you, I—

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: There never was any Supreme Anarchist Council,

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: We were all a lot of silly policemen looking at each other. And all these nice people who have been peppering us with shot thought we were the dynamiters. I knew I couldn’t be wrong about the mob, Vulgar people are never mad. I’m vulgar myself, and I know. I am now going on shore to stand a drink to everybody here.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: I can’t make head or tail of old Sunday’s little game any more than you can, But whatever else Sunday is, he isn’t a blameless citizen. Damn it! do you remember his face?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I grant you, that I have never been able to forget it.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Well,

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: I suppose we can find out soon, for tomorrow we have our next general meeting. You will excuse me, for being well acquainted with my secretarial duties.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I suppose you are right, I suppose we might find it out from him; but I confess that I should feel a bit afraid of asking Sunday who he really is.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Why, for fear of bombs?

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: No, for fear he might tell me.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Let us have some drinks,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I tell you I’ve seen him!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Whom?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Not the President?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Not so bad as that, not so bad as that. I’ve got him here.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Got whom here?

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Hairy man, man that used to be hairy man—Gogol. Here he is,

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Why do you worry with me?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You have expelled me as a spy.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: We are all spies!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: We’re all spies!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Come and have a drink.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: This is more cheerful, we are six men going to ask one man what he means.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I think it is a bit queerer than that, I think it is six men going to ask one man what they mean.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: My reason is quite simple, I attack him rashly because I am afraid of him.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Delightful!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: So pleased to see you all. What an exquisite day it is. Is the Czar dead?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: No, sir, there has been no massacre. I bring you news of no such disgusting spectacles.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Disgusting spectacles?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You mean Dr. Bull’s spectacles? Of course, we all have our opinions and even our eyes, but really to call them disgusting before the man himself—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: My spectacles are blackguardly, but I’m not. Look at my face.

speaker: the President
quoted_text: I dare say it’s the sort of face that grows on one, in fact, it grows on you; and who am I to quarrel with the wild fruits upon the Tree of Life? I dare say it will grow on me some day.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: We have no time for tomfoolery, We have come to know what all this means. Who are you? What are you? Why did you get us all here? Do you know who and what we are? Are you a half-witted man playing the conspirator, or are you a clever man playing the fool? Answer me, I tell you.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Candidates, are only required to answer eight out of the seventeen questions on the paper. As far as I can make out, you want me to tell you what I am, and what you are, and what this table is, and what this Council is, and what this world is for all I know. Well, I will go so far as to rend the veil of one mystery. If you want to know what you are, you are a set of highly well-intentioned young jackasses.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: And you, what are you?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I? What am I?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You want to know what I am, do you? Bull, you are a man of science. Grub in the roots of those trees and find out the truth about them. Syme, you are a poet. Stare at those morning clouds. But I tell you this, that you will have found out the truth of the last tree and the top-most cloud before the truth about me. You will understand the sea, and I shall be still a riddle; you shall know what the stars are, and not know what I am. Since the beginning of the world all men have hunted me like a wolf—kings and sages, and poets and lawgivers, all the churches, and all the philosophies. But I have never been caught yet, and the skies will fall in the time I turn to bay. I have given them a good run for their money, and I will now.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: There’s one thing I’ll tell you though about who I am. I am the man in the dark room, who made you all policemen.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Stop thief!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What about Martin Tupper _now?_

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What does the old maniac mean?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What does yours say, Syme?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No one would regret anything in the nature of an interference by the Archdeacon more than I. I trust it will not come to that. But, for the last time, where are your goloshes? The thing is too bad, especially after what uncle said.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: After him!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He can’t go astray now. There’s no mistaking a fire-engine.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Fly at once. The truth about your trouser-stretchers is known.—A FRIEND.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What place can this be?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Can it be the old devil’s house? I’ve heard he has a house in North London.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: All the better, we shall find him at home.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: No, but it isn’t that, I hear the most horrible noises, like devils laughing and sneezing and blowing their devilish noses!

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: His dogs barking, of course,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Why not say his black-beetles barking! snails barking! geraniums barking! Did you ever hear a dog bark like that?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: The dogs of Sunday would be no ordinary dogs,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, listen to that, is that a dog—anybody’s dog?

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Well, his house ought to be hell! and if it is hell, I’m going in!

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Why, you asses, it’s the Zoo!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Has it come this way?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Has what?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: The elephant!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: An elephant has gone mad and run away!

speaker: the other
quoted_text: He has run away with an old gentleman, a poor old gentleman with white hair!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: What sort of old gentleman?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: A very large and fat old gentleman in light grey clothes,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, if he’s that particular kind of old gentleman, if you’re quite sure that he’s a large and fat old gentleman in grey clothes, you may take my word for it that the elephant has not run away with him. He has run away with the elephant. The elephant is not made by God that could run away with him if he did not consent to the elopement. And, by thunder, there he is!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Stop him!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He’ll be out of the gate!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Stop a landslide!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He is out of the gate!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Great Lord!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I never knew an elephant could go so fast. Well, it must be hansom-cabs again if we are to keep him in sight.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: The word, I fancy, should be ‘pink’.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Where has he gone to?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Gentleman rushed into the Exhibition, sir! Funny gentleman, sir. Asked me to hold his horse, and gave me this.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: To the Secretary of the Central Anarchist Council.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: When the herring runs a mile, Let the Secretary smile; When the herring tries to _fly_, Let the Secretary die. Rustic Proverb.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Why the eternal crikey, did you let the man in? Do people commonly come to your Exhibition riding on mad elephants? Do—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Look!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Look over there!

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Look at what?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Look at the captive balloon!

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Why the blazes should I look at a captive balloon?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What is there queer about a captive balloon?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Nothing, except that it isn’t captive!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Ten thousand devils!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: He’s got into it!

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: God bless my soul!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: God bless my soul! I seemed to fancy that something fell on the top of my hat!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Your beauty has not left me indifferent.—From LITTLE SNOWDROP.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I’m not beaten yet. The blasted thing must come down somewhere. Let’s follow it!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: After all, it is very beautiful!

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: It is singularly and strangely beautiful!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I wish the beastly gas-bag would burst!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: No, I hope it won’t. It might hurt the old boy.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Hurt him! hurt him! Not as much as I’d hurt him if I could get up with him. Little Snowdrop!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I don’t want him hurt, somehow,

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: What!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Do you believe all that tale about his being our man in the dark room? Sunday would say he was anybody.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I don’t know whether I believe it or not, But it isn’t that that I mean. I can’t wish old Sunday’s balloon to burst because—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, because?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Well, because he’s so jolly like a balloon himself, I don’t understand a word of all that idea of his being the same man who gave us all our blue cards. It seems to make everything nonsense. But I don’t care who knows it, I always had a sympathy for old Sunday himself, wicked as he was. Just as if he was a great bouncing baby. How can I explain what my queer sympathy was? It didn’t prevent my fighting him like hell! Shall I make it clear if I say that I liked him because he was so fat?

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: You will not,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I’ve got it now, it was because he was so fat and so light. Just like a balloon. We always think of fat people as heavy, but he could have danced against a sylph. I see now what I mean. Moderate strength is shown in violence, supreme strength is shown in levity. It was like the old speculations—what would happen if an elephant could leap up in the sky like a grasshopper?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Our elephant, has leapt into the sky like a grasshopper.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: And somehow,

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: that’s why I can’t help liking old Sunday. No, it’s not an admiration of force, or any silly thing like that. There is a kind of gaiety in the thing, as if he were bursting with some good news. Haven’t you sometimes felt it on a spring day? You know Nature plays tricks, but somehow that day proves they are good-natured tricks. I never read the Bible myself, but that part they laugh at is literal truth, ‘Why leap ye, ye high hills?’ The hills do leap—at least, they try to.... Why do I like Sunday?... how can I tell you?... because he’s such a Bounder.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You do not know Sunday at all. Perhaps it is because you are better than I, and do not know hell. I was a fierce fellow, and a trifle morbid from the first. The man who sits in darkness, and who chose us all, chose me because I had all the crazy look of a conspirator—because my smile went crooked, and my eyes were gloomy, even when I smiled. But there must have been something in me that answered to the nerves in all these anarchic men. For when I first saw Sunday he expressed to me, not your airy vitality, but something both gross and sad in the Nature of Things. I found him smoking in a twilight room, a room with brown blind down, infinitely more depressing than the genial darkness in which our master lives. He sat there on a bench, a huge heap of a man, dark and out of shape. He listened to all my words without speaking or even stirring. I poured out my most passionate appeals, and asked my most eloquent questions. Then, after a long silence, the Thing began to shake, and I thought it was shaken by some secret malady. It shook like a loathsome and living jelly. It reminded me of everything I had ever read about the base bodies that are the origin of life—the deep sea lumps and protoplasm. It seemed like the final form of matter, the most shapeless and the most shameful. I could only tell myself, from its shudderings, that it was something at least that such a monster could be miserable. And then it broke upon me that the bestial mountain was shaking with a lonely laughter, and the laughter was at me. Do you ask me to forgive him that? It is no small thing to be laughed at by something at once lower and stronger than oneself.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Surely you fellows are exaggerating wildly, President Sunday is a terrible fellow for one’s intellect, but he is not such a Barnum’s freak physically as you make out. He received me in an ordinary office, in a grey check coat, in broad daylight. He talked to me in an ordinary way. But I’ll tell you what is a trifle creepy about Sunday. His room is neat, his clothes are neat, everything seems in order; but he’s absent-minded. Sometimes his great bright eyes go quite blind. For hours he forgets that you are there. Now absent-mindedness is just a bit too awful in a bad man. We think of a wicked man as vigilant. We can’t think of a wicked man who is honestly and sincerely dreamy, because we daren’t think of a wicked man alone with himself. An absentminded man means a good-natured man. It means a man who, if he happens to see you, will apologise. But how will you bear an absentminded man who, if he happens to see you, will kill you? That is what tries the nerves, abstraction combined with cruelty. Men have felt it sometimes when they went through wild forests, and felt that the animals there were at once innocent and pitiless. They might ignore or slay. How would you like to pass ten mortal hours in a parlour with an absent-minded tiger?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: And what do you think of Sunday, Gogol?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I don’t think of Sunday on principle, any more than I stare at the sun at noonday.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, that is a point of view, What do you say, Professor?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Wake up, Professor!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Tell us what you think of Sunday.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I think something, that I cannot say clearly. Or, rather, I think something that I cannot even think clearly. But it is something like this. My early life, as you know, was a bit too large and loose. “Well, when I saw Sunday’s face I thought it was too large—everybody does, but I also thought it was too loose. The face was so big, that one couldn’t focus it or make it a face at all. The eye was so far away from the nose, that it wasn’t an eye. The mouth was so much by itself, that one had to think of it by itself. The whole thing is too hard to explain. But put it this way. Walking up a road at night, I have seen a lamp and a lighted window and a cloud make together a most complete and unmistakable face. If anyone in heaven has that face I shall know him again. Yet when I walked a little farther I found that there was no face, that the window was ten yards away, the lamp ten hundred yards, the cloud beyond the world. Well, Sunday’s face escaped me; it ran away to right and left, as such chance pictures run away. And so his face has made me, somehow, doubt whether there are any faces. I don’t know whether your face, Bull, is a face or a combination in perspective. Perhaps one black disc of your beastly glasses is quite close and another fifty miles away. Oh, the doubts of a materialist are not worth a dump. Sunday has taught me the last and the worst doubts, the doubts of a spiritualist. I am a Buddhist, I suppose; and Buddhism is not a creed, it is a doubt. My poor dear Bull, I do not believe that you really have a face. I have not faith enough to believe in matter.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Have you noticed an odd thing, about all your descriptions? Each man of you finds Sunday quite different, yet each man of you can only find one thing to compare him to—the universe itself. Bull finds him like the earth in spring, Gogol like the sun at noonday. The Secretary is reminded of the shapeless protoplasm, and the Inspector of the carelessness of virgin forests. The Professor says he is like a changing landscape. This is queer, but it is queerer still that I also have had my odd notion about the President, and I also find that I think of Sunday as I think of the whole world.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Get on a little faster, Syme, never mind the balloon.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: When I first saw Sunday, I only saw his back; and when I saw his back, I knew he was the worst man in the world. His neck and shoulders were brutal, like those of some apish god. His head had a stoop that was hardly human, like the stoop of an ox. In fact, I had at once the revolting fancy that this was not a man at all, but a beast dressed up in men’s clothes.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Get on, And then the queer thing happened. I had seen his back from the street, as he sat in the balcony. Then I entered the hotel, and coming round the other side of him, saw his face in the sunlight. His face frightened me, as it did everyone; but not because it was brutal, not because it was evil. On the contrary, it frightened me because it was so beautiful, because it was so good.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Syme, are you ill?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It was like the face of some ancient archangel, judging justly after heroic wars. There was laughter in the eyes, and in the mouth honour and sorrow. There was the same white hair, the same great, grey-clad shoulders that I had seen from behind. But when I saw him from behind I was certain he was an animal, and when I saw him in front I knew he was a god.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Pan, was a god and an animal.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Then, and again and always, that has been for me the mystery of Sunday, and it is also the mystery of the world. When I see the horrible back, I am sure the noble face is but a mask. When I see the face but for an instant, I know the back is only a jest. Bad is so bad, that we cannot but think good an accident; good is so good, that we feel certain that evil could be explained. But the whole came to a kind of crest yesterday when I raced Sunday for the cab, and was just behind him all the way.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Had you time for thinking then?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Time, for one outrageous thought. I was suddenly possessed with the idea that the blind, blank back of his head really was his face—an awful, eyeless face staring at me! And I fancied that the figure running in front of me was really a figure running backwards, and dancing as he ran.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Horrible!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Horrible is not the word, It was exactly the worst instant of my life. And yet ten minutes afterwards, when he put his head out of the cab and made a grimace like a gargoyle, I knew that he was only like a father playing hide-and-seek with his children.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: It is a long game,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Listen to me, Shall I tell you the secret of the whole world? It is that we have only known the back of the world. We see everything from behind, and it looks brutal. That is not a tree, but the back of a tree. That is not a cloud, but the back of a cloud. Cannot you see that everything is stooping and hiding a face? If we could only get round in front—

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Look! the balloon is coming down!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: He is dead!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: And now I know he was my friend—my friend in the dark!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Dead!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You will not find him dead easily. If he has been tipped out of the car, we shall find him rolling as a colt rolls in a field, kicking his legs for fun.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: Clashing his hoofs, The colts do, and so did Pan.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Pan again!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You seem to think Pan is everything.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: So he is, in Greek. He means everything.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Don’t forget, that he also means Panic.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: It fell over there, Let us follow it! Oh, if he has cheated us all by getting killed! It would be like one of his larks.

speaker: the Secretary
quoted_text: Gentlemen, my master has a carriage waiting for you in the road just by.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Who is your master?

speaker: the man
quoted_text: I was told you knew his name, Where is this carriage?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It has been waiting only a few moments, My master has only just come home.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Show us the place,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: What can it all mean?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Is this another joke of Sunday’s?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I don’t know, but if it is, it’s one of the jokes you talk about. It’s a good-natured one.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Refreshments are provided for you in your room.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I have put out your clothes, sir.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Clothes!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I have no clothes except these,

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: My master asks me to say, that there is a fancy dress ball tonight, and that he desires you to put on the costume that I have laid out. Meanwhile, sir, there is a bottle of Burgundy and some cold pheasant, which he hopes you will not refuse, as it is some hours before supper.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Cold pheasant is a good thing, and Burgundy is a spanking good thing. But really I do not want either of them so much as I want to know what the devil all this means, and what sort of costume you have got laid out for me. Where is it?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You’re to be dressed as Thursday, sir,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Dressed as Thursday!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It doesn’t sound a warm costume.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: Oh, yes, sir, the Thursday costume is quite warm, sir. It fastens up to the chin.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Well, I don’t understand anything, I have been used so long to uncomfortable adventures that comfortable adventures knock me out. Still, I may be allowed to ask why I should be particularly like Thursday in a green frock spotted all over with the sun and moon. Those orbs, I think, shine on other days. I once saw the moon on Tuesday, I remember.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Beg pardon, sir, Bible also provided for you,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: This is getting wilder and wilder, Who are these people who provide cold pheasant and Burgundy, and green clothes and Bibles? Do they provide everything?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Yes, sir, everything, Shall I help you on with your costume?

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: Oh, hitch the bally thing on!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: We do not know yet that he is not dead in a field.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: We will eat and drink later, Let us remain together a little, we who have loved each other so sadly, and have fought so long. I seem to remember only centuries of heroic war, in which you were always heroes—epic on epic, iliad on iliad, and you always brothers in arms. Whether it was but recently (for time is nothing), or at the beginning of the world, I sent you out to war. I sat in the darkness, where there is not any created thing, and to you I was only a voice commanding valour and an unnatural virtue. You heard the voice in the dark, and you never heard it again. The sun in heaven denied it, the earth and sky denied it, all human wisdom denied it. And when I met you in the daylight I denied it myself. But you were men. You did not forget your secret honour, though the whole cosmos turned an engine of torture to tear it out of you. I knew how near you were to hell. I know how you, Thursday, crossed swords with King Satan, and how you, Wednesday, named me in the hour without hope.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Who and what are you?

speaker: the other
quoted_text: I am the Sabbath, I am the peace of God.

speaker: the other
quoted_text: I know what you mean, and it is exactly that that I cannot forgive you. I know you are contentment, optimism, what do they call the thing, an ultimate reconciliation. Well, I am not reconciled. If you were the man in the dark room, why were you also Sunday, an offense to the sunlight? If you were from the first our father and our friend, why were you also our greatest enemy? We wept, we fled in terror; the iron entered into our souls—and you are the peace of God! Oh, I can forgive God His anger, though it destroyed nations; but I cannot forgive Him His peace.

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: No, I do not feel fierce like that. I am grateful to you, not only for wine and hospitality here, but for many a fine scamper and free fight. But I should like to know. My soul and heart are as happy and quiet here as this old garden, but my reason is still crying out. I should like to know.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: It seems so _silly_ that you should have been on both sides and fought yourself.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I understand nothing, but I am happy. In fact, I am going to sleep.

speaker: the Professor
quoted_text: I am not happy, because I do not understand. You let me stray a little too near to hell.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I wish I knew why I was hurt so much.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: I have heard your complaints in order. And here, I think, comes another to complain, and we will hear him also.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Gregory!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Why, this is the real anarchist!

speaker: Gregory
quoted_text: Yes, I am the real anarchist.

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: ‘Now there was a day,’

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: ‘when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them.’

speaker: Gregory
quoted_text: You are right, I am a destroyer. I would destroy the world if I could.

speaker: Gregory
quoted_text: Oh, most unhappy man, try to be happy! You have red hair like your sister.

speaker: Gregory
quoted_text: My red hair, like red flames, shall burn up the world, I thought I hated everything more than common men can hate anything; but I find that I do not hate everything so much as I hate you!

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I never hated you,

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: You!

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: You never hated because you never lived. I know what you are all of you, from first to last—you are the people in power! You are the police—the great fat, smiling men in blue and buttons! You are the Law, and you have never been broken. But is there a free soul alive that does not long to break you, only because you have never been broken? We in revolt talk all kind of nonsense doubtless about this crime or that crime of the Government. It is all folly! The only crime of the Government is that it governs. The unpardonable sin of the supreme power is that it is supreme. I do not curse you for being cruel. I do not curse you (though I might) for being kind. I curse you for being safe! You sit in your chairs of stone, and have never come down from them. You are the seven angels of heaven, and you have had no troubles. Oh, I could forgive you everything, you that rule all mankind, if I could feel for once that you had suffered for one hour a real agony such as I—

speaker: Syme
quoted_text: I see everything, everything that there is. Why does each thing on the earth war against each other thing? Why does each small thing in the world have to fight against the world itself? Why does a fly have to fight the whole universe? Why does a dandelion have to fight the whole universe? For the same reason that I had to be alone in the dreadful Council of the Days. So that each thing that obeys law may have the glory and isolation of the anarchist. So that each man fighting for order may be as brave and good a man as the dynamiter. So that the real lie of Satan may be flung back in the face of this blasphemer, so that by tears and torture we may earn the right to say to this man, ‘You lie!’ No agonies can be too great to buy the right to say to this accuser, ‘We also have suffered.’ “It is not true that we have never been broken. We have been broken upon the wheel. It is not true that we have never descended from these thrones. We have descended into hell. We were complaining of unforgettable miseries even at the very moment when this man entered insolently to accuse us of happiness. I repel the slander; we have not been happy. I can answer for every one of the great guards of Law whom he has accused. At least—

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Have you, have you ever suffered?

speaker: Unknown
quoted_text: Can ye drink of the cup that I drink of?
